title: Labeled Jars in a Studio Apartment
analogy: A variable is like a mason jar labeled with a sharpie. You can store loose change (numbers), your crush's name (text), or relationship status (true/false). Clear labels ensure you don't confuse sugar with salt.
question: Complete the code below so the 'balance' variable holds the number 50000 (not text):
codeSnippet:
let balance = ___;
console.log(balance);
explanation: Numbers do not need quotation marks. If you write "50000" with quotes, the computer treats it as TEXT. The difference is critical: 50000 + 1 is 50001, but "50000" + 1 is "500001". Imagine if that happened to your bank balance!
hint: Write the pure number without wrapping it in quotation marks.

title: Passport ID vs Digital Wallet
analogy: 'const' is like your Passport number — once assigned, it never changes. 'let' is like your digital wallet balance — fluctuating daily with every coffee run.
question: You are coding a POS cash register. Store name never changes, but order total changes with each scanned item. Which declaration is correct?
explanation: Lock the store name with 'const' to prevent accidental renames. Use 'let' for orderTotal because it changes. Reassigning a const throws 'Assignment to constant variable'. Golden rule: default to const, use let only when reassignment is needed.
hint: Permanent values get locked. Dynamic values stay flexible.

title: Dynamic Names on a Checkout Receipt
analogy: A template literal is like an automated receipt stamp with placeholder slots. Slot the customer's name right into the hole instead of manual glue-and-scissor string concatenation.
question: Complete the code to output 'Hello Alex, your balance is 50000':
explanation: Inside backticks (`), embed variables with ${variableName}. Both the dollar sign and curly brackets are required. Omitting the dollar sign prints literal text '{name}'.
hint: Dollar sign first, then wrap the variable in curly braces.

title: Checking Wallet Balance Before Ride Request
analogy: If/Else is the security guard at the gate. 'If you have a badge, welcome in. If not, sign the visitor log.' Zero ambiguity — strictly two paths.
question: Ride fare is 12000. Which condition correctly checks if balance is sufficient?
explanation: Use >= (greater than or equal to). If balance exactly equals fare, the order still goes through. Don't confuse '=' (assignment), '=>' (arrow function), and '>=' (comparison).
hint: Equal balance is still valid. 'Greater than' first, then 'equals'.

title: Bug Hunt: Passwords Always Pass
analogy: A single '=' is overwriting an exam paper instead of grading it. Triple '===' is actually comparing the student's answer to the master key.
question: This bug allows anyone to log in, even with incorrect credentials. Where is the vulnerability?
options: Line 1: actualPassword should be let instead of const
Line 7: else does not need braces
explanation: A single '=' overwrites actualPassword with userInput. The assignment evaluates to truthy, bypassing authentication! Always use strict equality '==='.
hint: Count the number of equals signs inside the conditional parentheses.

title: Supermarket Shelves Starting at Zero
analogy: An array is a row of grocery shelves. Crucially, the first shelf is NOT number 1 — it is index 0. Programmers count from zero, just like ground floors in European elevators.
question: How do you retrieve 'Iced Tea' from this shopping cart?
codeSnippet:
let cart = ["Noodles", "Eggs", "Iced Tea", "Chips"];

console.log(___);
explanation: Counting: Noodles=0, Eggs=1, Iced Tea=2, Chips=3. The index is 2. This is the classic 'off-by-one' trap in software engineering.
hint: First item is index 0. What index is the 3rd item?

title: Adding Items to Shopping Cart
analogy: push() is dropping an item into your shopping basket — it appends right onto the back of the line automatically.
question: Complete the code to append 'Instant Coffee' to the end of the cart array:
explanation: push() adds items to the tail of an array. pop() removes the last item, shift() takes from the front, and unshift() inserts at the front. In JS, there is no .add() or .append() for Arrays.
hint: In English, you 'push' the item into the queue.

title: Calling Roll Room by Room
analogy: A loop is like a property manager knocking on apartment doors one by one to collect rent. The manager stops when all doors have been checked. If they forget to stop, they knock forever (infinite loop).
question: Complete the loop condition so all tenant names are printed without errors:
explanation: Use '<' instead of '<='. Length is 3, but the last valid index is 2. With '<=', tenants[3] would be accessed, printing 'undefined'. Using .length dynamically adapts as items are added.
hint: The last index is always length minus one. Never include the equals sign.

title: Bug Hunt: POS Register Prints No Receipt
analogy: A function without 'return' is an ATM that calculates your cash withdrawal internally but never dispenses the money through the slot. The work happened, but you walk away empty-handed.
question: This code prints 'undefined' instead of 27000. What is missing?
options: The function must be called twice
The total variable must use const
explanation: The function calculates 25000 + 2000 = 27000, but without 'return', JavaScript implicitly returns 'undefined'. Add 'return total;' to pass the output back.
hint: The calculation was completed, but never shipped out of the function.

title: Updating Website Billboard Banners
analogy: The DOM is your web page room. querySelector is your hand pointing to the exact item to grab, and textContent is the marker writing a new message.
question:
Given

Loading...

, which code correctly changes the text to 'Welcome'?
codeSnippet:
// HTML:

Loading...

___
explanation: Three rules: start with 'document', prefix ID selectors with '#', and assign to textContent with '='. Omitting '#' makes the browser look for an HTML tag named <headline>.
hint: IDs are selected with a '#' symbol. Assign with '=', not parentheses.

title: Doorbell Waiting to be Pressed
analogy: addEventListener is installing a doorbell. You don't know when guests will arrive, but the instant someone rings, the indoor chime sounds. Your code listens patiently rather than chasing.
question: Complete the code to trigger when the button is clicked:
explanation: Event names are clean verbs like 'click', without the 'on' prefix. 'onclick' is only for inline HTML attributes, which is considered legacy practice.
hint: Drop the 'on'. Just the bare action verb.

title: Bug Hunt: Forms Fleeing Before Data is Sent
analogy: HTML forms have an ancient reflex: upon submit, they immediately reload the page. preventDefault() is grabbing the collar to keep it grounded until data is sent.
question: Each time the form is submitted, the page refreshes and data is lost. What is missing?
options: Missing 'e.preventDefault();' on the first line inside the handler
Variable email should use let instead of const
correctAnswer: Missing 'e.preventDefault();' on the first line inside the handler
explanation: Parameter 'e' is the event object. Calling e.preventDefault() stops the browser's default form submission page reload, preserving your asynchronous JavaScript logic.
hint: Parameter 'e' is received but never told what to prevent.

title: Ordering Food via Delivery App
analogy: fetch() is tapping 'Order' on your delivery app. The food does not instantaneously materialize on your table — you receive an order confirmation. That confirmation is a Promise: a guarantee that data is on its way.
question: Why does console.log print 'Promise { <pending> }' instead of data?
options: Because fetch is asynchronous; result must be unwrapped with .then() or await
Because data should be declared with let
correctAnswer: Because fetch is asynchronous; result must be unwrapped with .then() or await
explanation: Network requests take time. JavaScript doesn't freeze the UI; it returns a Promise immediately. Status <pending> means the request is in flight. Use await or .then() to resolve.
hint: Consider the latency between clicking 'Order' and food arriving on your desk.

title: Unwrapping the Takeout Box
analogy: A server Response is like food sealed inside a cardboard takeout box. .json() is opening the lid. Until you unbox it, you are holding packaging, not the meal.
question: Complete the code to parse raw server data into a JavaScript object:
explanation: response.json() transforms raw response stream into a traversable JavaScript object. Notice two .then() calls: first unboxes the stream, second consumes the parsed data.
hint: Standard web data format abbreviation: JavaScript Object Notation.

title: Waiting for Water to Boil
analogy: await is standing in front of the kettle waiting for water to boil. Execution pauses cleanly on that line without moving on to brewing until water is boiling.
question: Complete the two keywords so this asynchronous function executes correctly:
explanation: Strict syntax: 'async' decorates the function declaration, granting permission to use 'await' inside its body. Await without async triggers a syntax error.
hint: Function declaration gets the permit, network call gets the pause command.

title: Bug Hunt: White Screen When Wifi Drops
analogy: try/catch is a safety helmet. You don't plan to crash, but if you hit unexpected terrain, your app survives intact. Without it, a single offline glitch crashes the whole app into a blank white screen.
question: When the server is offline, the entire UI blanks out without feedback. What is missing?
options: Needs try/catch block to gracefully intercept network failures
Missing semicolon at the end of line
fetch should use .then() instead of await
Function must be called inside window.onload
correctAnswer: Needs try/catch block to gracefully intercept network failures
explanation: When network drops or server returns 500, await throws an unhandled rejection. Wrap in try { ... } catch (err) { showError("Network disconnected"); } to inform users gracefully.
hint: Any code communicating over external networks requires a fallback safety harness.

title: Waiting Room Number Board
analogy: State is a digital ticket display board in a clinic. Whenever the number updates, every patient in the waiting room notices and looks up. Changing a private notepad does nothing for the room.
question: Why does the screen number stay at 0 even though the variable incremented?
options: Regular variables do not trigger React re-renders; must use useState
onClick must be written in lowercase
correctAnswer: Regular variables do not trigger React re-renders; must use useState
explanation: 'count' incremented in JavaScript memory, but React was never notified to re-render the DOM. const [count, setCount] = useState(0) triggers the React render pipeline.
hint: React needs an official notification to repaint the screen.

title: Bug Hunt: Cart Items Not Updating Onscreen
analogy: Modifying state with push() is scribbling on an already-photocopied checklist — the original changed, but everyone holding the old copy sees nothing new. React checks if the array address changed; if identical, it skips re-rendering.
question: Items enter the array in console logs, but the UI list stays empty. Why?
options: Must create a NEW array reference: setItems([...items, item])
correctAnswer: Must create a NEW array reference: setItems([...items, item])
explanation: push() mutates the array in place, keeping the identical memory address. React performs a shallow check (prev === next) and cancels re-rendering. Spread syntax [...items, item] creates a new array reference.
hint: Never mutate existing arrays. Generate a fresh array container.

title: Data Warehouse Access Card
analogy: createClient produces an access keycard for your data warehouse. You need two pieces: the warehouse address (URL) and your credentials (anon key). Missing either will block entry at the guardhouse.
question: Complete the Supabase client setup in Next.js:
explanation: createClient(url, anonKey) instantiates the Supabase client. Keys are read from environment variables to avoid hardcoding secrets in source control.
hint: Matches the exact name imported on line 1.

title: Ordering Items from the Warehouse
analogy: A Supabase query is like instructing a waiter: 'From the menu table (.from), give me name and price (.select), but only items in stock (.gt).' The sequence is structured and readable.
question: Which query correctly retrieves 'name' and 'price' from 'products' where stock > 0?
codeSnippet: const { data, error } = await ___;
explanation: Method chaining order: .from() specifies table, .select() specifies columns, followed by filter predicates (.gt, .eq, .lt). Always destructure and verify error before consuming data.
hint: Specify the table source first, then select columns and filters.

title: Bug Hunt: Data Writes Silently Failing
analogy: This is transferring money and closing the banking app without checking the receipt. If the transfer failed due to insufficient funds or network drops, you would never know until customers complain.
question: User data occasionally fails to save, but the app still displays 'Saved Successfully'. Why?
options: The 'error' object is never checked before reporting success
insert requires an array instead of an object
correctAnswer: The 'error' object is never checked before reporting success
explanation: Supabase does not throw exceptions on query failures; it returns an { error } object. You must check: if (error) throw error; before displaying success messages.
hint: Look at the variable retrieved on line 2 that is ignored thereafter.

title: Server Component vs Client Component
analogy: A Server Component is the executive chef in the back kitchen — holding vault keys and secret recipes, delivering only finalized dishes to the table. A Client Component is the dining room server — interacting directly with guests (clicking, typing), but never holding vault secrets.
question: You are building an interactive like button with useState. What directive is required at the top?
options: "use client" at the very top of the file
"use server" at the very top of the file
correctAnswer: "use client" at the very top of the file
explanation: App Router components default to Server Components. To use browser APIs, event handlers, or React hooks (useState, useEffect), you must declare "use client" as the first statement.
hint: Interactive components belong to the browser client.

title: Setting Up Your Own API Endpoint
analogy: A Route Handler is a customer service counter you set up yourself. It has a sign (route.ts), operating hours (GET/POST methods), and serves every incoming request with a formal Response.
question: Complete the API handler in app/api/chat/route.ts to accept incoming POST payloads:
explanation: In App Router, exported function names correspond directly to HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). Exporting POST handles incoming payload submissions.
hint: HTTP method used to send data payloads to a server.

title: Bug Hunt: AI API Key Leaked Globally
analogy: Putting secret API keys in client-side code is taping your ATM PIN to the back of the debit card. Convenient, but anyone holding the card can empty your account. In web development, 'anyone' means any user opening Chrome DevTools.
question: This code works, but your API bill explodes unexpectedly within 48 hours. What caused the leak?
options: API key prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC in a client component, exposing it to anyone in DevTools
Method should be GET instead of POST
correctAnswer: API key prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC in a client component, exposing it to anyone in DevTools
explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ bundles secrets into JavaScript sent to browsers. Anyone can read it in Network or Sources tabs! Rule: never expose secrets on client; route AI requests through secure server Route Handlers.
hint: Examine the environment variable prefix. One word means 'exposed to the public'.
